articles.headline: The surprising leadership dynamics in agent swarms
articles.blurb: Agent swarms are groups of agents that work together to accomplish a task. Researchers created an experiment in which eight agents from four different models worked together to resolve simulated outages to understand how agents organize themselves in a swarm without a designated leader. They discovered two factors that could influence an agent's potential leadership: the agent's underlying models, and the order in which their name was listed in a prompt. This suggests that even seemingly minor details in how an agent swarm is configured can affect how agents coordinate.

articles.headline: Droid 1.0: Building a Frontier Harness

It's hard to separate real progress from adaptations to that model's quirks when you tune against a single model. Working across models ensures the strongest improvements generalize and hold up beyond the model that inspired them.

articles.headline: Why Sam Altman is against a single superintelligence

Swarms of agents match a lot of the properties of a resilient society. They keep each other in check and collaborate to work towards goals. AI research shouldn't lead in a centralized direction because agents pushing against each other creates a dynamic equilibrium.

AI can send hordes of superhumanly fast, well-read, and mathematically gifted researchers to accelerate scientific research. It is possible AI will enable new types of discovery and ways of understanding the natural world that no network of humans would ever be able to discover. Unless humans have actually somehow discovered most of the actual exploitable regularities in the Universe, we're about to enter a new golden age of science.

articles.headline: A Little Determinism
articles.blurb: Adding constraints to AI agents usually makes them less capable. Sometimes the solution is to create a template or a complete multi-stage workflow. The challenge is in creating the deterministic behavior while retaining the agent's freedom to use the best tools for the job. This post discusses a solution that uses a man-in-the-middle egress proxy that forces behavior by denying actions and forces reactions via automated messages.

articles.headline: Making agents fast - what I've learnt over the last 12 months
articles.blurb: Knowing what part of inference a project relies on for speed is important. Check thinking budgets, and read traces, as they often contain valuable insight into what an agent wants to do. Give agents the tools they want rather than what you think they need. Faster hardware still matters, sandboxing and microVMs add complexity, parallelization helps, and classic software performance optimization is still relevant.

articles.headline: How JD.com Built a Lakestream with Apache Fluss and Apache Hudi
articles.blurb: JD replaced parallel streaming and batch training-data pipelines with a staged migration: write once to Fluss, tier to Hudi, and union fresh plus historical reads. The difficult part is consistency: workers coordinate a single Hudi commit per tiering round and report matched stream offsets only after it completes. That pattern enables rollback-safe catch-up, but leaves schema evolution and dynamic bucketing unresolved.

articles.headline: The paper that split the database in four: inside Azure SQL Database Hyperscale, aka Socrates
articles.blurb: Azure SQL once kept four full copies of each database, which capped practical size at around 4 TB. The 2019 Socrates paper separated the log from storage, so durability and availability could scale apart. This change in approach let Hyperscale reach 100 TB, halve storage copies, and restore a 50 TB database in minutes.

articles.headline: The 2026 Cloud Data Warehouse Benchmark (Website)

Databricks had the smallest latency increase from 1 GB to 1 TB (3.7x versus MotherDuck's 30x), with tuning and autoscaling disabled throughout.

articles.headline: Best Practices for Single Row Lookups (Point Queries)
articles.blurb: DataFusion can perform surprisingly well on point lookups when tuned for retrieval instead of analytics. The biggest gains came from storage layout and execution choices that minimize unnecessary work, such as sorted Parquet files, right-sized row groups, metadata caching, and prepared statements. The broader lesson is that analytical engines can serve low-latency reads if the workload is designed deliberately.

articles.headline: Getting an analytics agent from 50% to 96% accuracy

articles.headline: The Benchmarking Crisis
articles.blurb: AI code generation is helping database engines game ClickBench. One, pgrust, groups strings by hash value alone, caches predicates the benchmark repeats, and on one query skips most of the data. Any benchmark stops being useful once systems optimise for it, and vibe-coded engines have no customers to keep them honest.

articles.headline: Egres: A Postgres-compatible database for heavy, multi-tenant workloads
articles.blurb: What would Postgres look like if designed today? Egres is the answer: a new open-source database that speaks the Postgres protocol but shares almost no Postgres code. It runs thousands of tenants in one process, metering CPU, memory, and disk per query, and its benchmark used 46% less disk than Postgres 18.

articles.headline: Gems of DuckDB 2.0.0
articles.blurb: DuckDB 2.0 adds a Python appender for batching generated rows, CLI function manuals and queryable command history, plus secure views that hide underlying statistics and query plans. Other additions include custom partition paths, sorting within exported partitions, direct GeoJSON exports, and support for extension-defined window functions.

articles.headline: SLayer (GitHub Repo)
articles.blurb: SLayer is an MIT-licensed, embeddable semantic layer for governed agent and human access to warehouse data through MCP, REST, SQL, or Python. It combines read-only connectivity, SQL translation, transformations, row-level security, semantic search, and memory, and imports dbt, Cube, or Ossie definitions. Its expression model supports ratios, time shifts, and multi-stage queries beyond fixed BI metrics.

articles.headline: PrivacyLib: Privacy Controls at the Data Access Boundary
articles.blurb: Meta built PrivacyLib to enforce privacy rules at the moment data is accessed, replacing one-off integrations with shared controls that work across many systems. The key lesson is to normalize diverse data platforms into a small set of common operations, which makes policy enforcement reusable, scalable, and adaptable enough to extend from traditional infrastructure to AI agents.

articles.headline: DuckDB Universe (Tool)

Entries include GitHub star counts and source links, with examples ranging from PyGWalker and Evidence to MotherDuck and DeepSeek's smallpond.

articles.headline: Making Failure Diagnosis Reliable with Pensive AI
articles.blurb: Netflix made failure diagnosis more reliable by using LLMs to identify the exact log spans behind an error and provide on-demand root-cause analysis, instead of asking models to digest entire logs. That design improved coverage to all failures while reducing hallucination risk and latency, and early usage data suggests it sharply cuts manual log exploration during debugging.

articles.headline: Reducing BigQuery Costs Through Its Biggest Problem: The Users
articles.blurb: An open-source BigQuery FinOps agent cuts waste from user-written SQL by detecting common cost mistakes, rewriting queries, and validating savings before execution.

articles.blurb: Flink's Kafka connector now reconciles checkpoint state with Kafka's actual position, preventing misleading offsets on transactional topics and making its committed-offset metric match Kafka tooling without weakening exactly-once processing.

articles.blurb: Google's AI search experience keeps shoppers within its own ecosystem, especially for fashion and beauty products. A study of 55,198 AI answers found that 57% of product links led to Google Shopping and 46.5% of US product answers linked only to Google pages. Brands may gain visibility in AI search without receiving website traffic.

articles.headline: What marketers should know about the legal risks of algorithmic pricing
articles.blurb: Dynamic pricing, where every customer sees the same demand-driven price, is relatively safe, but pricing that changes based on the shopper carries much greater legal risk. A promo code sent to one segment or a retargeted offer that undercuts the public price can count as personalized pricing. Dozens of bills are pending across more than 20 states, and the FTC has drafted a policy statement on when the practice is misleading or unfair. False-advertising laws also apply, since a sale price only some shoppers see may misrepresent the discount.

articles.headline: Drive more app downloads for $0
articles.blurb: Turn high-engagement UGC comments into app downloads by replying to questions about problems your app solves. Read the comment on camera, answer it, show the relevant app feature, then tell viewers where to download it. One family meal-planning app used this tactic to generate 100K+ views on a reply to a post with 8M+ views and 16K comments.

articles.headline: How to Implement & Measure Viral Loops: Stories from SaaS Growth Experts
articles.blurb: The most sustainable viral loops in SaaS come from invites the product already requires, not from asking users to refer someone. A QR code generator labels every free code so each real-world scan exposes the brand, while an assessment tool reaches new users whenever a recruiter invites a candidate. K-factor sums every loop into one growth rate, and the useful inputs are invite-accept rate and invitee activation rather than opens or clicks. Gating rewards on activation and fixing activation first keep the loop fueled, since users who never reach value have nothing to share.

articles.headline: Instagram just launched long-form video…but I don't think brands should use it
articles.blurb: Instagram's new long-form video format isn't a priority for brands that haven't mastered short-form content. Brands should first create Reels over 60 seconds that earn strong watch time and engagement, then turn successful formats into consistent series that build an audience. Long-form is worth exploring only when short videos can persuade viewers to watch more. Create content that builds brand influence and drives action, not just views.

articles.blurb: Reddit is shifting toward a primarily logged-in experience as AI-powered search reduces traffic from Google and other search engines. The move aims to limit AI scraping and encourage data-licensing deals while giving Reddit more user data to personalize feeds and target ads. Search referrals fell by more than 1M per week in October, while daily active users in the US dropped 2% year over year to 50.7M. Reddit will test the change in select markets outside the US in Q4.

articles.headline: The horror movie marketing hall of fame
articles.blurb: Horror campaigns have to hook audiences without giving the scare away, usually on small budgets. The Blair Witch Project and Longlegs built worlds with fake websites and real-world touchpoints that turned curiosity into word of mouth. Backrooms tapped a fandom that already existed online rather than starting from scratch. Smile planted actors with creepy grins at sports broadcasts and earned about 170 million trackable impressions without buying airtime. Obsession made its villain feel real with a text-me billboard and her own Letterboxd account, turning a $750K budget into $522M worldwide.

articles.headline: How Brands Make Boring Industries Desirable
articles.blurb: Categories where shoppers once bought whatever was cheapest or on the shelf leave more room for a brand to change how the whole category feels. Jolie positions its filtered showerhead against skincare rather than plumbing, while Scrub Daddy's smiling face doubles as the sponge's grip and its social personality. Making a commodity feel premium, designing it to be left out, or turning its use into a ritual gives buyers a reason to care which brand they pick in a category where that choice barely mattered.

articles.headline: More Americans Have Tried Crypto, But Few Are Sticking With It
articles.blurb: A survey of 1,545 US adults, commissioned by the DeFi Education Fund, shows lifetime crypto ownership rising to 22% from 18%, yet active past-year usage held flat at 13%, pointing to a retention problem more than an awareness gap. The lifetime figure grew because lapsed users returned: among respondents who had not used crypto in the past year, 11% reported prior ownership, up from 5% a year ago, while new-user entry did not accelerate. Trust in crypto exchanges (4% high trust) and decentralized platforms (5%) sits far below the 42-48% high-trust ratings earned by banks and credit unions, and DeFi familiarity registers at just 2% "very familiar." Despite the GENIUS Act establishing federal stablecoin rules, stated interest in learning about stablecoins fell to 7% from 11%, and DeFi interest dropped to 8% from 11%, showing that regulatory clarity has not translated into consumer engagement.
